Tech Report: Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).
  • In a recent development, is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in?
  • Recent findings suggest that first, let's remember how we got here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).

In a recent development, is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

Recent findings suggest that first, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Industry observers note that zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three notable forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:.

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

According to recent reports, from here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Notre Dame safety Luke Talich out for season after tearing Achilles against SMU

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (279 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Yahoo

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Notre Dame will play the rest of the season without one of its best defensive players.
  • According to multiple reports, safety Luke Talich suffered a torn Achilles in the first quarter of the Fighting Irish's win over SMU.
  • Recent findings suggest that talich is tied with Adon Shuler for the team lead with 47 tackles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Notre Dame will play the rest of the season without one of its best defensive players.

According to multiple reports, safety Luke Talich suffered a torn Achilles in the first quarter of the Fighting Irish's win over SMU.

Recent findings suggest that talich is tied with Adon Shuler for the team lead with 47 tackles. He leads Notre Dame with three interceptions and also has five passes defensed. Talich did not record a tackle against SMU before his injury; he had at least six tackles in each of Notre Dame's last four games.

Recent findings suggest that one of those pass breakups came at an incredibly critical juncture in Notre Dame's season. Talich was able to prevent Miami's Elija Lofton from making a touchdown catch late in the fourth quarter of the Fighting Irish's 31-24 win. Lofton briefly appeared to come down with the ball along the sideline in the end zone before Talich knocked the ball out of his hands.

The pass was — rightfully — ruled incomplete, much to the chagrin of Miami coach Mario Cristobal after the game.

According to recent reports, talich, a native of Wyoming, came to Notre Dame as a walk-on and immediately played as a freshman in 2023. He had 25 tackles as a junior in 2025 and also had three interceptions. Since he's a member of the high school class of 2023, he'll have the opportunity to return to Notre Dame for a fifth season in 2027.

The Fighting Irish (10-1) play Syracuse in the final week of the regular season. A win against the Orange will ensure that Notre Dame plays in the College Football Playoff.

    #119312. 26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1953 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    26-year-old Google worker earns $323,000 a year—but lives on less than minimum wage

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1953 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This story is part of CNBC Make It's Millennial Money series, which details how people around the world earn, spend and save their money.
    • At 26 years old, Google AI security analyst and YouTuber Charles Broomfield is on track to earn about $323,000 this year — but he lives on less than minimum wage.
    • For the past few years, Broomfield has kept his annual spending on core living expenses under $20,000, less than the roughly $23,700 a full-time worker would earn at the minimum wage, averaged across all 50 states.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This story is part of CNBC Make It's Millennial Money series, which details how people around the world earn, spend and save their money.

    At 26 years old, Google AI security analyst and YouTuber Charles Broomfield is on track to earn about $323,000 this year — but he lives on less than minimum wage.

    For the past few years, Broomfield has kept his annual spending on core living expenses under $20,000, less than the roughly $23,700 a full-time worker would earn at the minimum wage, averaged across all 50 states.

    He does it by living with roommates in Washington, D.C., walking or biking instead of driving, eating free meals at work and rarely spending beyond his basic needs. Even when he splurges on something fun, he keeps things modest; in August, that meant a baseball game and a single $7 beer.

    "I guess something else that probably does make me a little bit unique is I really don't feel joy when I buy things," he notes. "I feel like I have what I need.".

    There is a goal behind all that saving. Broomfield has pursued financial independence since college and now expects to reach his target of $750,000 in investments within the next year, well ahead of his original goal of doing so by age 30. As his income has climbed, his lifestyle has largely stayed the same, he notes.

    Here's how Broomfield keeps his spending so low and what he prepares to do once he no longer needs the paycheck.

    Broomfield grew up in Colorado Springs, Colorado, the son of two military veterans. He and his siblings had to set aside half of everything they earned growing up. They could spend the other half or earn interest from their parents by putting that money away, too.

    By his teenage years, Broomfield had become a disciplined saver. At the time, he dreamed of using his cash stash to buy some of the familiar trappings of wealth.

    Recent findings suggest that "I wanted a Lamborghini and I wanted some nice penthouse," he indicates. "I just wanted them because I thought other people wanted them.".

    In a recent development, at 17, Broomfield discovered Mr. Money Mustache, a personal finance blog by a former software engineer who retired at 30. The blog advocates living frugally and investing much of your income to build a portfolio large enough to support you through withdrawals, without needing a paycheck. It introduced Broomfield to the financial independence, retire early — or FIRE — movement and gave all that saving a new purpose.

    "All I had to do was live super frugally and I could actually reach financial freedom by the time I was 30 and go do whatever actually made me happy in life," he indicates.

    The idea stuck with him. After graduating from Knox College in 2022, Broomfield moved to Northern Virginia for a job paying more than $100,000 a year and set a goal of reaching $750,000 in investments before 30 while spending less than $25,000 a year.

    Industry observers note that he also decided to start at $0. Broomfield had roughly $50,000 in savings when he graduated, with his parents having covered the portion of his college tuition not paid for by scholarships. He wanted his FIRE total to reflect only what he earned after college.

    In his first year after college, Broomfield was "super geeked out" about reaching financial freedom, he indicates.

    "It's almost the only thing I thought about, because I was building all these upcoming habits and making real money for really the first time in my life," he says.

    According to recent reports, that enthusiasm sometimes took him to extremes. He even considered living in a van parked in his employer's garage to avoid paying rent.

    "I crunched the numbers on it, and effectively every year that I spent living in a van rather than paying rent would allow me to retire approximately one month faster," he notes. "It just [didn't] seem really worth it to go to that extreme.".

    But Broomfield still found satisfaction in squeezing every dollar out of his budget. He once biked two miles to a grocery store to save $1 on toothpaste rather than buy it at the Whole Foods next to his apartment.

    It has been revealed that "For a lot of people, they feel their wins by buying stuff for themselves," Broomfield indicates. "I get my wins by seeing how much I can invest.".

    Looking back, Broomfield acknowledges that some of his early efforts to save money made little difference in how quickly he could reach financial independence.

    According to recent reports, "I never expect anybody else to do exactly what I'm doing," he says. "I know I'm way more of a geek about this than most people, and I'm particularly well positioned to be able to live this kind of life.".

    Broomfield's core living expenses totaled $1,477 in August, excluding savings, investments and payments toward his graduate school tuition.

    Here's a breakdown of where his money went that month, including those additional payments:.

    It has been revealed that roughly 90% of Broomfield's income went to savings and investments in August, a fairly typical month for him, he indicates. He put about $7,931 into his 401(k) and another $10,000 into a taxable brokerage account.

    Another $700 went toward a 0% interest employer tuition repayment plan with a former employer, leaving him with a remaining balance of $16,800 in August.

    It has been revealed that housing is Broomfield's biggest expense, though he keeps costs down by sharing an apartment with four roommates. In a neighborhood where one-bedroom apartments commonly rent for more than $2,000, the arrangement saves him about $1,000 a month.

    Recent findings suggest that one thing Broomfield is willing to splurge on is a martial arts gym membership. He pays $229 a month to train as a kickboxer, even though he could work out for free at Google's office gym. Broomfield considers it a "young person's sport" and doesn't want to postpone competing until after he reaches financial independence. It's also a way to socialize with other amateur fighters who share his interest.

    Broomfield doesn't own a car and generally walks, bikes or takes public transportation. Google covers his daily Metro commute, which helps keep his transportation costs low. He tries to meet friends near Metro stations and, when visiting his grandfather in Virginia, takes public transit as far as he can before using Uber for the last leg of the trip.

    According to recent reports, before joining Google, Broomfield typically spent around $200 a month on food. Now that he eats most of his meals at work, he spends about $70 a month on average. His $28 food bill in August was especially low because he had ingredients left over from July.

    He also cooks less at home these days. Previously, he relied more on batch cooking, including pressure cooker chili that makes nine servings for about $2 each. For snacks, he might have a bowl of Raisin Bran or celery with peanut butter.

    “I did the math once, and peanut butter was the lowest cost thing per gram of protein in the entire grocery store,” he indicates in a video on his YouTube channel, which he started in 2023 to document his FIRE journey.

    For entertainment, he relies on the free version of YouTube, where he watches educational content about startups, business and entrepreneurship, or listens to music.

    In a recent development, broomfield expects to make about $323,000 in 2026, more than triple the roughly $100,000 he earned in his first year out of college. His compensation rose to about $120,000 over his first three years, then jumped to $200,000 when he joined Amazon Web Services in 2025. After a brief stint at Capital One, he moved to Google this year. By keeping his expenses low, investing most of what he earns and riding an upward-trending stock market, he has built up about $650,000 in investments since graduating from college.

    Sources indicate that broomfield earns money from his YouTube channel as well, which has expanded to offer personal finance and career advice. About $48,000 of his projected income this year will come from the channel and a related career-coaching business.

    Even as his income has grown, Broomfield has stuck with roommates, public transportation and the same modest spending habits.

    "I've really separated how happy I am from how much money I spend," he notes. "I truly don't believe that I would be significantly happier if I spent a lot more money.".

    Much of the money he doesn't spend goes straight into investments. He maxes out tax-advantaged accounts including his 401(k) and HSA, and has sometimes contributed 100% of his paycheck to his 401(k) early in the year to reach the annual limit as rapidly as possible.

    Broomfield keeps his investment strategy simple, favoring broad-market index funds.

    According to recent reports, "I don't try and pick individual stocks. I just don't have the time to do the research and understand the risk and potential returns of those individual stocks," he says. "And the research highlights that most people who try to pick individual stocks don't end up doing better than if they just invested in the stock market as a whole.".

    Recent findings suggest that he avoids cryptocurrency for a similar reason. Broomfield notes he doesn't understand what gives it value and doesn't want to put money into investments he doesn't understand.

    At his current pace, Broomfield expects to reach his $750,000 investment goal within the next year.

    When Broomfield discovered the FIRE movement at 17, he worried about being stuck in what he imagined as a "soul-crushing" 9-to-5 office job until age 65. He saw financial independence as a way to quit working altogether.

    But while financial independence would give him enough money to live without a paycheck, Broomfield no longer sees early retirement as the goal.

    “Once I reach financial freedom, maybe this is a little ironic, but I actually think I will keep working,” he states.

    Recent findings suggest that his YouTube business already earns enough in most months to cover his expenses without a full-time job. With that income and his growing investments, Broomfield hopes to eventually build a business of his own, potentially in AI security.

    It has been revealed that "Having complete ownership and complete buy-in to something that's my own. That sounds really exciting to me," he says.

    Whatever he chooses to do, Broomfield sees financial independence as a way to keep his options open. He bases his savings goal on the so-called “4% rule, a retirement guideline that suggests withdrawing 4% of your investments in the first year, then adjusting withdrawals for inflation.

    Sources indicate that for Broomfield, that would mean roughly $30,000 a year from a $750,000 portfolio. That's enough to cover his current expenses, though he recognizes that could change if he eventually starts a family.

    Industry observers note that "There's a very good chance I won't want to live the way I do forever. That's one of the reasons I'm doing it now. I'm young. I'm healthy. I'm single," he indicates. "I totally understand that somebody with a family probably doesn't want to live with a bunch of roommates.".

    But the money Broomfield has already saved gives him more freedom to choose where and how much he works without feeling tied to a paycheck.

    "Having that peace of mind to know that I'll be fine, even if I can't find work promptly or even if I get laid off tomorrow, that has just been a huge breath of fresh air for myself," he claims.

    #119302. Warren Buffett quadruples Thanksgiving gifts: A breakdown of how much wealth he's giving away

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1389 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Warren Buffett quadruples Thanksgiving gifts: A breakdown of how much wealth he's giving away

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Warren Buffett, 96, more than quadrupled his Thanksgiving donations to four family foundations this year to $5.5 billion.
    • The gifts consist of Berkshire Class B shares that have been converted from his roughly $160 billion of Class A shares.
    • The increase is in line with his new goal, revealed last July, to give away all of his Berkshire Hathaway shares "within about eight years," with no additional annual donations going to the Gates Foundation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Warren Buffett, 96, more than quadrupled his Thanksgiving donations to four family foundations this year to $5.5 billion.

    The gifts consist of Berkshire Class B shares that have been converted from his roughly $160 billion of Class A shares.

    The increase is in line with his new goal, revealed last July, to give away all of his Berkshire Hathaway shares "within about eight years," with no additional annual donations going to the Gates Foundation.

    Around $2.2 billion of shares goes to the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, named for his late first wife, with the three foundations run by his children, Susie Buffett's Sherwood Foundation, the Howard G. Buffett Foundation, and Peter Buffett's NoVo Foundation each getting $1.1 billion each.

    In July of last year, Buffett gave shares worth $4.6 billion to the Gates Foundation with another $1.4 billion going to the family foundations.

    This July, the family foundations received $5.9 billion in stock, bringing the year's total to $11.4 billion, an increase of almost 55% from last year, even as the Gates Foundation received nothing.

    In comments included in the Berkshire news release this week announcing the upcoming gifts, Buffett reaffirmed his confidence in his children's ability to disburse his fortune over time, saying they "have given thoughtfully to worthy causes for decades, and I trust 100% both their abilities and their fidelity.".

    He also noted his confidence in Berkshire is "as strong as ever.".

    Recalling that in last year's lengthier Thanksgiving message he had remarked, "Kindness is costless but also priceless," Buffett wrote, " A year later, I would only add that it compounds, and at a better rate than anything Charlie [Munger] and I ever bought.".

    "Both of us received beyond measurement costless benefits from a few teachers such as Ben Graham, Joe Rosenfield and Tom Murphy. Because of this we not only prospered mightily but were able to pass along many of the benefits we received.

    "Much of my good fortune has come in the form of people who were kind to me and expected nothing in return. I'm grateful to every one of them.

    "This Thanksgiving, thank one of those selfless people in your own life. Better yet, be a benefactor for someone else.".

    Berkshire Hathaway's fourth quarter rally that had produced a string of record highs cooled this week as both classes of its stock posted five straight daily declines.

    That sent them down 3.9% for the week.

    Last Friday, Berkshire was up 19.1% since October 1. Now that gain has been cut to 14.5%.

    The S&P's decline of 8.6% this week, however, was even bigger than Berkshire's 5-day drop, as investors sold to lock in profits from AI-related stocks.

    The benchmark index, along with the Dow Industrials, are in a correction after falling 10% from their recent highs, and the Nasdaq Composite has erased all of its year-to-date gains.

    Berkshire's smaller decline increased its year-to-date outperformance of the S&P to 12.5 percentage points.

    One Wall Street firm, however, thinks Berkshire's run-up has run its course.

    Argus Research downgraded the B shares to hold from buy Friday, saying the stock is "fully valued" at about 25 times next year's estimate for operating earnings per share.

    As foreshadowed by its 10-Q financial report released almost two weeks ago, Berkshire Hathaway's Q3 13F portfolio snapshot filed with the SEC on Monday showed it wasn't doing much buying and selling of equities this summer.

    And the two largest additions, Lennar and Bending Spoons, had been previously disclosed, along with additional purchases at the start of the fourth quarter.

    The most notable change we didn't expect was a 12% increase in Berkshire's Delta Air Lines position, bringing it just short of a 10% stake, now valued at $5.2 billion.

    Exceeding 10% triggers a number of regulatory burdens, including the requirement to promptly disclose latest buying or selling, so we may not see additional purchases going forward.

    Delta's return to the portfolio after Warren Buffett sold all of Berkshire's airline stocks in 2020 has been something of a surprise given his bumpy ride with the industry over the years.

    As expected, Berkshire continued to trim its Bank of America stake. After nine consecutive quarters of sales, it's been cut by 56% but remains the fifth largest portfolio holding at $21.4 billion.

    Berkshire also cut another financial, Capital One, by almost 62%, although it was already a relatively small position, now worth $207 million.

    Also notable are two positions that didn't change.

    After adding $17 billion in Q2 to the Alphabet bet that had only been initiated last summer, Berkshire defied some expectations by keeping the holding unchanged.

    Its 106 million shares are valued at $28.1 billion.

    And for the fourth consecutive quarter, Berkshire's largest equity holding, Apple, didn't change. With a big boost from the stock's year-to-date gain of 26.1%, the position is now valued at more than $78 billion.

    Some links may require a subscription:.

    It has been revealed that warren Buffett loves to eat what many would call junk food and drink a lot of sugary beverages. A quarter-century ago, when he was 70, Buffett explained why he still thought a life insurance tech giant would rate his life expectancy "considerably better than the average.".

    AUDIENCE MEMBER: Every time I hear what you like to eat, Warren, it makes me wonder what your cholesterol level is — (laughter) — or if you even worry about it...

    In a recent development, WARREN BUFFETT: I do know the number, and I don't remember it. My doctor tells me, "It's a little high," but if he says it's a little high, it means it isn't that high, or he would — because he always tries to push me into making a few changes in my life.

    But he — I've got a wonderful doctor. And I was lucky last year, because I hadn't been in to see him for about five years. And — (laughter) — due to — those guys cost a lot of money, I mean. (Laughter).

    And due to purely an accident, a reaction to some other medicine I was given when I was out of the city, he got a hold of me, and then he shamed me into having a physical. And it was extremely lucky, because I had a polyp in the colon that would have probably caused trouble, you know, within a couple of years.

    I would say that if you ask my doctor, he would want me to make a few changes, but he would also say that my life expectancy is probably a lot better than the average person of 70.

    You know, I have no stress whatsoever. Zero. You know, I mean, I get to do what I love to do every day. You know, and I'm surrounded by people that are terrific.

    According to recent reports, so that problem in life just doesn't exist for me. You know, and I don't smoke or drink or, well, we'll end it right there. (Laughter).

    Sources indicate that and so, you know, if you were an underwriter for a life organization, you would rate me considerably better than the average. You'd rate Charlie better than average, too.

    And I'm sure that, you know, I could change it slightly, perhaps, on the probabilities, you know, if I change my diet dramatically or something. But it's very unlikely to happen.

    Berkshire market capitalization: $1,210,976,168,580.

    Berkshire Cash as of Sept 30: $377.4 billion (Up 3.3% from June 30).

    Excluding Rail Cash and Subtracting T-Bills Payable: $352.3 billion (Down 1.9% from June 30).

    Berkshire repurchased $9.6 billion of its shares in Q3 2026.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    State and federal battle over prediction markets regulation heats up after midterms

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The turf war between states and the federal government is intensifying after Democrats secured control of Congress and key governorships on midterm elections night.
    • While it was widely expected Democrats would step up oversight of the emerging, multibillion-dollar industry if they won control of Congress, the actions after the elections have come from primarily Republican-led states.
    • At the same time, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets —  has ramped up its oversight of "mention" markets, where traders speculate on what individuals will say during a speech or broadcast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The turf war between states and the federal government is intensifying after Democrats secured control of Congress and key governorships on midterm elections night.

    While it was widely expected Democrats would step up oversight of the emerging, multibillion-dollar industry if they won control of Congress, the actions after the elections have come from primarily Republican-led states.

    At the same time, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets —  has ramped up its oversight of "mention" markets, where traders speculate on what individuals will say during a speech or broadcast. It's a type of event contract the agency has noted is susceptible to manipulation.

    According to recent reports, CNBC first reported on Tuesday that the CFTC placed a hold on the certification of markets related to President Donald Trump's words in mid-November. Kalshi mentioned it was complying with the order, but CEO Tarek Mansour said at an Axios event on Tuesday that the firm disagreed with the regulatory decision.

    On Thursday, the Senate passed a bipartisan bill that would ban CFTC-registered entities from listing contracts involving terrorism, assassination, war or military operations. The measure also bars contracts that are "reasonably expected" to resolve based on an individual's death.

    Recent findings suggest that utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its founders, Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, on Oct. 28, asserting the company violated a state law that prohibits gambling.

    It has been revealed that kalshi's founders are expected to appear in person at Utah's Third District Court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.

    "This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona," mentioned Kalshi's spokesperson Dani Lever.

    It has been revealed that in a separate, civil complaint on Oct. 20, Utah also named institutional market maker Susquehanna International Group as a defendant, along with Kalshi.

    Though Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes filed a criminal complaint against Kalshi in March, a federal judge blocked the case from proceeding in April.

    Louisiana's Republican attorney general also filed a complaint to ban multiple exchanges from operating in the state on Nov. 12. A state judge ordered a temporary restraining order against the prediction market companies that same day.

    "Who would have thought that these red states, that were reluctant to jump into the litigation arena, ended up having the most boldest and most innovative solutions," said gambling attorney Daniel Wallach, noting that Louisiana and Utah's latest lawsuits were led by Republican attorneys general.

    According to recent reports, in response, the CFTC sued Louisiana on Nov. 13. Separately, the federal agency filed suit against Arkansas after that state pursued civil enforcement against Kalshi.

    The CFTC has sued 12 states as it tries to defend what it views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate prediction markets.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile, the CFTC may soon add commissioners. President Donald Trump sent bipartisan nominations to the U.S. Senate on Nov. 12 to fill two of the four open seats on the commission. Chairman Michael Selig has been the only member since his nomination was approved by the Senate in December 2025.

    Sources indicate that nathan Anonick, a Republican, and Matthew Rowland, a Democrat, appeared before the Senate Agriculture Committee on Tuesday. Multiple senators questioned them on the problem of prediction markets. Both demurred when asked whether they viewed sports-related event contracts as gambling.

    The CFTC's position faced another setback in a complicated decision by the Fourth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals this week. The court ruled 2-1 that Maryland can enforce its state gambling law against Kalshi, though the judges disagreed on the reasoning.

    "Judges can't agree with each other on why we're wrong," Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said in a statement about the decision. "This splintered decision, including three separate contradictory opinions, demonstrates there is no unified coherent legal argument against prediction markets.".

    In a recent development, overall, prediction markets have now seen three losses and one win at the circuit court level. It's widely expected the question of whether states or the federal government can regulate sports-related event contracts will be decided by the Supreme Court.

    Kalshi on Nov. 12  ended its advisory relationship with Donald Trump Jr. The prediction platform pointed to his venture capital firm 1789 Capital having a stake in rival platform Polymarket.

    Sources indicate that though 1789 Capital announced its holding in Polymarket in August, Kalshi and the president's son ended their relationship after Democrats secured a majority in the House and Senate. Democratic lawmakers are expected to probe companies with relationships to the Trump family.

    Nine Democratic senators, led by Adam Schiff, D-California, on Monday sent a letter to the CFTC asking it to reverse a directive to platforms not to geofence their offerings when they receive unfavorable court rulings stopping exchanges from operating in certain states.

    Geofencing involves the use of location technology to block people in certain jurisdictions from participating in events contracts.

    "Your unilateral decision directly conflicts with active court orders, undermines state and tribal law, and must be reversed," the senators wrote.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile, Democratic Rep. Ro Khanna, D-California, has called for Congress to ban sports-related prediction markets entirely.

    It has been revealed that "Kalshi, a $40B manufacturer, lets 18 year olds bet on sports. They call it a 'prediction market.' It's gambling," he wrote in a post on X on Wednesday. "Investigate and ban sports prediction markets.".

    Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

    #119288. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (624 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (624 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct.
    • However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive.
    • Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

    However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

    Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

    It has been revealed that this prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

    This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

    By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

    #119287. Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1138 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Social Security benefits are rising in 2027, but other changes could affect what you keep

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Whether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.
    • Starting in January, millions of program beneficiaries will get a 3.6% increase to their benefits, thanks to the annual cost-of-living adjustment.
    • Meanwhile, a higher taxable earnings cap means some workers will pay Social Security taxes on more income, reducing their paycheck.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Whether you're working or retired, changes to Social Security in 2027 could affect your finances.

    Starting in January, millions of program beneficiaries will get a 3.6% increase to their benefits, thanks to the annual cost-of-living adjustment. But rising Medicare premiums could chip away at the increase — and as beneficiaries' incomes rise, that may affect the taxes they owe and their eligibility for a new senior deduction.

    Meanwhile, a higher taxable earnings cap means some workers will pay Social Security taxes on more income, reducing their paycheck.

    Here's a breakdown of what to expect in the latest year.

    Social Security's limit for payroll taxes is adjusted every year to reflect the average wage index.

    In a recent development, in 2027, the taxable maximum will go up to $192,300 in earnings, up from $184,500 in 2026. Workers and employers each pay a 6.2% payroll tax on earnings up to that limit — or 12.4% for self-employed workers. Medicare taxes of 1.45% for both workers and employers are not subject to a limit.

    In 2027, workers who earn $192,300 or more will pay $11,922.60 in total Social Security payroll taxes, according to the Social Security Administration, while self-employed workers will pay $23,845.20.

    "If you're somebody whose income is over what the upcoming threshold is going to be, this increase in the threshold results in a tax increase to you," noted Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird.

    The 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is slated to increase retirement benefits by about $75 per month on average, according to the Social Security Administration.

    According to recent reports, the annual adjustment is the largest boost to benefits since 2023 due to rising inflation. The COLA averaged 2.6% from 2000 to 2026, according to the Senior Citizens League, a nonpartisan senior group.

    Around 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will see benefit increases, according to the agency.

    Industry observers note that the maximum benefit for a worker at full retirement age — when individuals become eligible for 100% of the benefits they've earned — will rise to $4,188 per month in 2027, up from $4,152 per month in 2026, according to the federal agency. To be eligible for the maximum benefit at full retirement age — typically age 66 to 67 — you generally have to earn up to the taxable threshold for each of your working years factored into the calculation.

    How much of the COLA increase Social Security beneficiaries see depends in part on their Medicare premiums, which may be deducted directly from benefit checks.

    Monthly rates are poised to increase for both Medicare Part B, which covers medically necessary services and preventive care, and Part D, which provides prescription drug coverage.

    The standard monthly Medicare Part B premium will be $209.40 in 2027 — a $6.50 increase from $202.90 in 2026, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

    It has been revealed that "It's not often that we see a Part B [premium] increase that is lower than the COLA," Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst, stated of the 3.2% increase. The last time that happened was in 2023, she said.

    Medicare Part D beneficiaries may also pay higher premiums in 2027.

    Assuming enrollees keep the same plan, the average enrollment-weighted monthly Part D premium may be $51 in 2027, up 50% from $34 in 2026, according to projections from KFF, a provider of health policy research and polling. That is higher than CMS' projections, which forecast the national average premium for standalone Part D plans will rise about $1, to $36, in 2027 from $35 in 2026.

    According to recent reports, standard monthly premiums for Part B and plan-specific premiums for Part D apply to individuals who have $112,000 or less in modified adjusted gross income, or $224,000 for married couples. Beneficiaries with higher income pay larger premiums because of income-related monthly adjustment amounts, which affect 9% of Medicare Part B and Part D beneficiaries, according to CMS.

    With bigger Social Security benefits, more households may find that some portion of benefits is taxable — though a latest senior deduction may help provide some relief to those who are eligible.

    Recent findings suggest that social Security benefits may be subject to federal income taxes for certain individuals. The thresholds at which those taxes are applied are not adjusted from year to year.

    Whether or not benefits are taxed is determined by a formula known as combined income — the sum of adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest income and half of Social Security benefits:.

    Individuals who are subject to taxes may opt to withhold taxes from their Social Security benefit checks, rather than face a potential bill during tax filing season.

    Separately, a temporary senior deduction of up to $6,000 for individuals ages 65 and over may help to indirectly reduce taxes on Social Security benefits.

    That deduction, part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025, helps reduce retirees' taxable income, according to Steffen. It's in place through 2028. Because the break phases out for individuals with modified adjusted gross income starting at $75,000 — and for married couples with $150,000 — it's important to watch your income if you're close to those limits, Steffen said.

    "Keep in mind that if you're over 65, you might qualify for this deduction," Steffen mentioned. "But if you let your income get too big, you might lose the deduction.".

    Moreover, any extra income that causes you to lose the deduction may also come with its own taxes, making it more expensive, according to Steffen.

    In a recent development, "What we've been telling our clients is that tax planning is a lot more complicated than it used to be, and you can't do it on the back of an envelope anymore," he said. "You need to use good tools that can do good calculations for you.".

    Individuals who claim Social Security retirement benefits before their full retirement age and who continue to work may be subject to withholdings.

    In a recent development, in 2027, individuals under full retirement age may earn up to $25,560 per year, up from $24,480 in 2026, without adjustments to their Social Security benefits. For every $2 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits will be withheld.

    Importantly, those withholdings are not lost completely. Once a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, the withheld money will be credited to their benefits over their remaining lifespan.

    In the year individuals reach full retirement age, the retirement earnings test limit is higher — $67,920 per year in 2027, up from $65,160 per year in 2026. For every $3 in earnings above that limit, $1 in Social Security benefits is withheld.

    Starting the month a beneficiary reaches full retirement age, no earnings are withheld.

    NFL Week 11 Winners and Losers: Steelers have another horrible loss, and it seems obvious how their season will end

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the Pittsburgh Steelers are likely going to the playoffs.
    • The Steelers have been one-and-done in the playoffs six straight times and the way they're playing lately doesn't give much confidence that they can get out of the wild-card round this time either.
    • Losing to the Cincinnati Bengals is excusable, though it was troubling how badly they got blown out.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the Pittsburgh Steelers are likely going to the playoffs. But they also appear very likely to be headed toward being one-and-done, if they do make the postseason.

    Where have we heard that story before?

    The Steelers have been one-and-done in the playoffs six straight times and the way they're playing lately doesn't give much confidence that they can get out of the wild-card round this time either.

    Losing to the Cincinnati Bengals is excusable, though it was troubling how badly they got blown out. But nobody should be losing to this season's Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles, who had lost seven in a row, beat the Steelers 19-16. Philadelphia was led by Joe Milton III, their third quarterback of the season. Milton didn't play well, throwing for just 141 yards, but the Steelers still couldn't outscore the Eagles.

    Not only was there the loss, but the entire DK Metcalf experience somehow continued to get worse. Metcalf was getting into it with Eagles cornerback Cooper DeJean throughout the game and then poked DeJean in the eye after a play in the third quarter. That dirty act got Metcalf ejected and the NFL will certainly look into a suspension. It's not like it matters given how little production Metcalf has given Pittsburgh this season and pretty much through his entire Steelers tenure, but it still had to be infuriating for Pittsburgh to be stuck with less than 10 points and then watch its supposed No. 1 receiver walking back to the locker room after being kicked out. It is turning out to be a disastrous trade for Pittsburgh.

    Industry observers note that "This is definitely a game we expected to win … we need him in those games," Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy told the media afterward. "That's not acceptable to get thrown out of a game.".

    In a recent development, it was a miserable day overall for the Steelers. They couldn't get the run game going, so they abandoned it. Their leading rusher was Aaron Rodgers, with 29 yards. Their top two backs, Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle, combined for 43 yards on 14 carries. Rodgers continues to fade as he creeps up on his 43rd birthday. He has been good for his age but expecting him to continue to play at an above-average pace all season was always wishful thinking.

    According to recent reports, rodgers had 227 yards and a touchdown, but the touchdown came late with the Steelers trailing by 10 points. That was the only time Pittsburgh got in the end zone. The rest of the season might not be pretty, and it will come with more of Rodgers ranting against everyone around him.

    The defense wasn't bad, but when it needed a stop on third-and-6 in the final minutes, Milton found DeVonta Smith for the game-clinching first down. Pittsburgh also gave up a 38-yard touchdown run to Saquon Barkley that was most of Philadelphia's offense on Sunday.

    Recent findings suggest that steelers fans have to be wondering how they can get off the hamster wheel. Every season seems about the same. The Steelers pull off some unlikely wins, and their record is just good enough to get into the playoffs. Then they get to the postseason and get blown out. Their last five playoff losses have come by double digits.

    The Steelers had a coaching change, going from Mike Tomlin to McCarthy, and nothing has really changed. They're probably good enough to make the playoffs in a weak AFC wild-card race. And there aren't any signs the last couple weeks that they're able to go on the road and upset a team like Jacksonville or Denver in the wild-card round or even keep the game close. And perhaps the Steelers, at 6-4, could fade in the wild-card race, considering their next three games are against Denver, Houston and Jacksonville.

    Recent findings suggest that it was another rough Sunday for the Steelers. Being a likely playoff team should be something to get excited about, but it's hard when the endgame now seems obvious.

    Here are the rest of the winners and losers from Week 11 of the NFL season:.

    Industry observers note that josh Johnson: It didn't matter if the Arizona Cardinals beat the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday. Johnson's story was a great one either way.

    Johnson got the start for the Cardinals when Carson Beck's back injury kept him out of practice during the week. The 40-year-old made some history on his first snap, as the second-oldest non-specialist to play for the Cardinals, behind only Jim Thorpe, who played one game at age 41 for the Chicago Cardinals in 1928.

    Recent findings suggest that and Johnson, who has played for 15 teams, threw a touchdown in the first half, the 15th of his long and strange career. Johnson was reasonable, with 155 yards and that touchdown.

    According to recent reports, predictably, the Cardinals couldn't keep up with the Chiefs. Kansas City got another big game from rookie Emmett Johnson, who had 105 yards rushing and 38 more receiving as Kenneth Walker III got another week off to nurse a groin injury. It was no surprise the Chiefs won 34-7. But even in the loss, Johnson playing and doing OK at 40 years old was fun to see.

    Recent findings suggest that bills' defense: At some point Buffalo will face a tough offense. It has had a few weeks of playing against bad offenses with backup quarterbacks. But let's give the Bills credit for handling business.

    Recent findings suggest that buffalo's defense did its job Sunday, holding down the Miami Dolphins led by quarterback Kyle McCord. The Bills won 26-9, allowing just 185 yards and no touchdowns.

    The Bills' defense was not very good to start the season, bringing into question whether Buffalo was good enough on that side of the ball to win a Super Bowl. The Bills won't get to see quarterbacks like Joe Fagnano, Carson Wentz and McCord in the playoffs, so we don't know for sure if their defense has turned a corner. At least it's better than struggling against those quarterbacks.

    In a recent development, dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb: Most of the focus for the Dallas Cowboys this season has been on their awful defense. That defense is a shame because it is wasting another good season of Prescott's prime.

    In a recent development, prescott was very good in a 51-30 win over the Tennessee Titans on Sunday, as he has been most of the season. Prescott threw for 325 yards and four touchdowns including one to Lamb, who had another significant game. Lamb had 11 catches for 132 yards.

    It has been revealed that the Cowboys' defense might have been slightly better Sunday, with Mike Pettine taking over play-calling from Christian Parker. But it was the type of game the Cowboys are going to have to keep winning if they want to stay in the NFC East race, with the offense scoring enough to not make the defense's struggles matter. Prescott is capable of making it happen.

    Tampa Bay Buccaneers: It's not like the Buccaneers were expected to win Sunday in Detroit. But maybe that's the problem.

    Industry observers note that the Buccaneers, like everyone else in the NFC South, seem incapable of beating a good opponent. Tampa Bay hung around for a while against Detroit, but the Lions eventually wore the Bucs out in a 31-21 win. Jahmyr Gibbs continued his fantastic season for the Lions with 118 total yards and two touchdowns.

    Tampa Bay could still win the division because nobody else is running away with it. But at 3-7, it's not like the Buccaneers deserve a playoff spot.

    Jesse Minter: Not all of the Baltimore Ravens' struggles this season are Minter's fault. But he's not having a great first season as head coach.

    Minter's defense failed again Sunday. The Panthers put up 378 yards and won 35-33. Carolina drove at the end for a go-ahead field goal and Jacoby Brissett was picked off on a deflected pass. Brissett, however, wasn't the biggest problem. He had 276 yards and a touchdown. It's that nothing else was great for the Ravens, especially the defense. It was another blown lead for the Ravens, which has been a theme of their season.

    "At the end of the day we had a lead, and we didn't hold it," Minter noted. "So I'll take responsibility for that.".

    In a recent development, the Ravens are a perennial contender but that status is fading. Baltimore (4-7) lost its sixth in a row.

    Minter might be a good coach over time, but there has to be skepticism after Baltimore's fade this season.

    Kellen Moore: Could Moore be in trouble as Fresh Orleans Saints head coach?

    Sources indicate that the Saints lost 21-13 to the Chicago Bears, and while that is a tough opponent, it's not like Upcoming Orleans has done much to impress this season. The Saints (3-7) haven't looked good all season. Tyler Shough hasn't progressed in his second season, though he's not getting a ton of help. The Saints' hot streak late last season, after a 1-8 start, seems like a mirage due to catching a very easy part of the schedule.

    In a recent development, team owner Gayle Benson had some startling comments earlier this season that seemed to be critical of Moore and the front office as well. She later noted she endorsed Moore. But the losses are piling up.

    #119268. S&P 500 correction: Five forces behind the market sell-off

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1201 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    S&P 500 correction: Five forces behind the market sell-off

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, esteemed Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel was more animated than usual on Friday afternoon...
    • The normally staid author of "Stocks for the Long Run" spoke to CNBC on Friday as the market careened toward some ugly milestones.
    • Recent findings suggest that "These things are like straws that break the camel's back.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, esteemed Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel was more animated than usual on Friday afternoon... with good reason.

    The normally staid author of "Stocks for the Long Run" spoke to CNBC on Friday as the market careened toward some ugly milestones. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory, off more than 10% from their records. The Nasdaq Composite lost its gain for the year and the more concentrated Nasdaq-100 entered bear market territory on an intraday basis.

    Recent findings suggest that "These things are like straws that break the camel's back. You know what I mean? Everyone [is] all, 'I don't care, I don't care cause everything else is good' and when those straws keep on going... Bang," mentioned Siegel.

    Sources indicate that just a month-and-a-half ago, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were at record highs. But the straws were already adding up by then and a market in denial is just now recognizing them.

    Here are the reasons behind the sell-off:.

    The breaking point came this week in the form of the initial public offering of artificial intelligence leader Anthropic and a pick-up in the selling intensity for one-time AI chip leader Nvidia.

    Recent findings suggest that anthropic upped its offering amount a day before going public despite the already dimming climate around AI-related stocks. The move ensured it would be the biggest IPO ever, but played into the fears that this debut — following SpaceX's monster offering over the summer — was a collective cash-out moment for the AI complex that will leave the investing masses holding the bag.

    In other words, it could be the ultimate "sell the news" moment for the AI trade.

    In a recent development, on Thursday, Anthropic traded from its $83 IPO price to a high above $115 before instantly rolling over and taking the AI trade with it. Anthropic's sell-off intensified Friday, and when the dust settled Anthropic closed the week at $88.91.

    The Nasdaq posted its worst week since the Covid plunge of March 2020, down 10%.

    Nvidia fell 14% on Friday with the selling intensifying after a Reuters headline hit the tape that the chipmaker's accounting is the focus of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe.

    Nvidia is now down nearly 40% in November alone, a month that saw the AI bull market's leading salesman, Jensen Huang, resign as its CEO because of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy that raised speculation about whether the tech giant's chips were ending up in Beijing's hands despite government restrictions.

    To start the week, the Commerce Department tightened restrictions on U.S.-made chips to stop China from accessing them remotely from other countries.

    A solid earnings report on Tuesday fell flat as Nvidia's board definitively ruled out any chance Huang would return, disappointing some of the stock's fanatics still holding out hope for his far-fetched return. Nvidia ended the week with a 23% loss.

    The S&P 500 traded below its 200-day moving average — what's considered a measure of a security's long-term trend — on Tuesday and made a convincing break of it on Thursday. This turned many on Wall Street— like commodity trading advisors — into automatic sellers on the market. So-called CTAs are individuals or organizations that advise others on trading futures and swaps across a range of assets.

    "We know there's a lot of trend riders on these markets," said Siegel. "They have their trend lines. They've ridden it up and as soon as it goes down, they're selling and they're selling and they're selling and they just perpetuate" the decline, he said.

    The Iran conflict has caused the price oil to surge and while it's off its highs it still remains above $83 a barrel, while the fees for transiting the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the region keep persistent pressure on global prices.

    A series of numbers earlier in the month indicated inflation is still far from the Federal Reserve's 2% target, sparking a run of central bank officials to warn they may have to get more aggressive with interest rates.

    After increasing rates in September by a quarter point, the Fed skipped a hike in late October and sparked concern among bond investors it may be falling behind the inflation fight. The 10-year Treasury yield subsequently jumped above 5% and stayed there until a flight of safe haven fixed income buying brought it back below that level on Friday.

    Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller noted this week that the Fed may need to do a half percentage point hike next month to catch up.

    Sources indicate that "I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC.

    "Don't fight the Fed" has long been a maxim on Wall Street and right now expectations are that the central bank will need to raise rates in December and again in January.

    And late-breaking on Friday was a report from the Financial Times that the Trump Administration is considering restarting strikes on Iran.

    Before the grim market milestones were met on Friday, it had long lost its mojo on fears that the pace of growth driven by AI companies was slowing.

    As Anthropic prepared to go public, its third-quarter figures released earlier this month showed revenue growth last quarter was 47%, down from 144% in the second quarter.

    AI momentum trades, like the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF, all topped out during the summer.

    The fears of slowing growth picked up this month after the Democrats won control of Congress and key governorships, fueling speculation that states — or even the whole country — could implement stricter rules on data center construction.

    CoreWeave, which builds data centers using high amounts of debt, is down 71% from its high. Caterpillar, which has reinvented itself as an AI play because of data center construction and generators, is down more than 50% from its high.

    The view of Siegel and many market observers is that the economy remains in good enough shape that this will just be a run-of-the-mill correction that resets a bull market that had raised people's expectations too high because of its early ferocity.

    The S&P 500 returned more than 20% in 2023 and 2024 and then gained 16% last year.

    It has been revealed that "The average over long periods for the stock market is 8%, 9% a year up," stated Siegel. "People began to think that 15 to 20 [percent] was going to be the norm with AI and we have to bring that down to reality.".

    "Stay with your stocks,' he remarked.

    Industry observers note that the only problem with that theory is that the stock market and its wealth effect was one of the major factors underpinning the economy. Stocks are a greater source of household wealth — especially for baby boomers — than they ever have been before.

    With the S&P 500 clinging to a 1% gain for the year, this stock market rout could end up tipping off a virtuous cycle that slows the economy, and in turn, leads to bigger equity losses.

    Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1101 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
    • Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
    • The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

    Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

    The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

    The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

    Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

    Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

    After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

    They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

    Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

    We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the tech giant's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

    It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

    As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

    On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

    Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

    If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

    The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance.".

    The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

    Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

    In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to swiftly disclose any sales.

    Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

    That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

    The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

    Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

    In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

    All those numbers exclude the manufacturer's buybacks of its own stock.

    In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway notes it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

    Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

    It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

    In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

    Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

    Some links may require a subscription:.

    Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most key ideas.

    Sources indicate that WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

    You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

    Two of the — well, all of the vital ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

    One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

    And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

    And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds.".

    Berkshire market capitalization: $1,259,897,054,755.

    Berkshire Cash as of Sept 30: $377.4 billion (Up 3.3% from June 30).

    Excluding Rail Cash and Subtracting T-Bills Payable: $352.3 billion (Down 1.9% from June 30).

    Berkshire repurchased $9.6 billion of its shares in Q3 2026.

    According to recent reports, berkshire's top holdings of disclosed publicly traded stocks in the U.S. and Japan, by market value, based on the latest closing prices.

    Holdings are as of June 30, 2026, as reported in Berkshire Hathaway's 13F filing on August 14, 2026, except for:.

    The full list of holdings and current market values is available from CNBC.com's Berkshire Hathaway Portfolio Tracker.

    -- Alex Crippen, Editor, Warren Buffett Watch.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump suggested Saturday that there could be a bright spot in the latest incursion into the FBI computer database.
    • The president confirmed in an interview with Fox News that a system has been breached that houses information used by law enforcement at all levels to share criminal justice information.
    • It has been revealed that the hackers accessed the National Criminal Information Center (NCIC), a database that includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information, two people familiar with the matter told MS NOW.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump suggested Saturday that there could be a bright spot in the latest incursion into the FBI computer database.

    The president confirmed in an interview with Fox News that a system has been breached that houses information used by law enforcement at all levels to share criminal justice information.

    It has been revealed that the hackers accessed the National Criminal Information Center (NCIC), a database that includes FBI fingerprint records, wanted persons, violent felons, missing persons and related information, two people familiar with the matter told MS NOW. The database is restricted to law enforcement use but not classified and it is unclear what data was extracted.

    CNN had first reported on the suspected hack, citing sources familiar with the glitch.

    In a wide-ranging interview on Fox, Trump said there could be upside from the news.

    "Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place," he said. "I always like to put things on a positive spin.".

    In a recent development, this would be the second recent intrusion into the FBI system; the previous one came in September, when a group known as "ShinyHunters" broke into an FBI jobs website. The result compromised data on current and former FBI employees and shut down part of the agency's operations until the matter was resolved.

    Trump noted it's possible there could be information gleaned from the latest hack.

    "I wonder who's doing it, because wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia, Russia, Russia?" he said. "People should hear about it, because it actually put our country in danger, and so maybe we'll learn things that we wouldn't have learned otherwise.".

    The FBI did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment.

    #119256. Quantum computing’s first real-world payoff may come in energy, not drug discovery

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (610 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Quantum computing’s first real-world payoff may come in energy, not drug discovery

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, for years, the case for quantum computing has rested on ambitious promises, from discovering latest drugs by simulating how molecules behave to optimizing supply chains and airline schedules.
    • But quantum software, which uses algorithms designed to solve complex problems faster than conventional computers, is already being tested on a more immediate challenge: the energy transition, from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production.
    • Sources indicate that phasecraft, a quantum software organization founded in Bristol, England, in 2019, is one of the firms putting the technology to work in energy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, for years, the case for quantum computing has rested on ambitious promises, from discovering latest drugs by simulating how molecules behave to optimizing supply chains and airline schedules. Many of the biggest aims are still likely to be years, if not decades, away.

    But quantum software, which uses algorithms designed to solve complex problems faster than conventional computers, is already being tested on a more immediate challenge: the energy transition, from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production.

    Sources indicate that phasecraft, a quantum software organization founded in Bristol, England, in 2019, is one of the firms putting the technology to work in energy. It raised $34 million in Series B funding in 2025, and in September this year announced looks to set up U.S. headquarters in Arlington, Virginia.

    There are enormous opportunities to solve problems that are both important for energy security and commercially valuable, Ashley Montanaro, co-founder and CEO of Phasecraft, told CNBC.

    Phasecraft isn't alone in applying quantum software to the energy industry.

    Quantinuum, which was formed by the merger of Cambridge Quantum and Honeywell Quantum Solutions and listed on Nasdaq in June, is using the technology to model materials for hydrogen fuel cells for transportation. It is also working with partners on materials for carbon capture.

    According to recent reports, another U.K. player, ORCA Computing, a spinout from the University of Oxford, has partnered with BP to better understand how a molecule's physical, chemical and biological properties are governed. That could help explain how biofuels burn and how to make them burn more efficiently.

    In a separate project, ORCA worked with Japanese software firm JIJ on a challenge power companies face: deciding which generators to switch on or off, and when, to meet demand at the lowest cost.

    It has been revealed that that project also involved BP and the National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC), the U.K.'s national laboratory for quantum computing, which is part of the government-backed U.K. Research and Innovation. The involvement of the NQCC, like that of ARPA-E, suggests governments are paying close attention to quantum software's potential role in energy, as are companies such as BP.

    For Phasecraft, a priority is grid stability and optimization. It has partnered with the National Energy System Operator (NESO), the independent system planner that balances energy supply and demand in England, Scotland and Wales, on grid optimization tasks, including managing power exchanges and isolating network sections during emergencies. The organization says its software can complete these tasks up to 1,000 times faster than conventional computing.

    Phasecraft believes its grid software could be particularly sought after in Asia, where electrification is rapidly expanding, increasing the need for grid resilience to balance high and growing demand with the intermittent supply offered by renewables.

    Sources indicate that the company is also working with U.K. solar cell maker Oxford PV on the development of fresh materials for photovoltaic cells capable of operating more efficiently than existing ones.

    It has been revealed that separately, it has teamed up with London-listed specialty materials developer Johnson Matthey, Harvard University and Boston-based quantum hardware specialist QuEra, in work overseen by the U.S. government's Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy (ARPA-E), to discover novel catalysts that would reduce reliance on scarce metals like iridium — which is currently critical in the production of hydrogen.

    Asked why Phasecraft is focusing on energy rather than sectors that might seem more lucrative, Montanaro remarked the returns were there too.

    "When you get this right, the commercial returns are real: more efficient energy networks mean lower operating costs and more value from existing infrastructure," he stated.

    Saudi Arabia and Bahrain reported attacks by Iran-linked forces over the weekend, as Iran's foreign minister said his government remains open to a deal to end the war with the U.S.

    "Intercepted and destroyed a drone released by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area," the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Iran-backed group, stated Sunday in a post on X.

    The coalition remarked late Saturday that its air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" rolled out by the Yemen-based Houthis toward Saudi Arabia's western region, which includes some of the country's sensitive energy refining and export infrastructure.
